utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and Happy New Year to you and everyone in and around the courtroom. Barney Thomas appearing for the Prosecution together with Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Happy New Year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I trust that everyone had an decent break and some calm and some rest. I understand that Mr. Thomas certainly did and I'm pleased about that. Appearing on behalf of the Defence today are Mr. Novak Lukic, Tina Drolec, Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair. I'm Gregor Guy-Smith and we have a new intern working with us today that's Mr. Eric Tully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thomas any housekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No housekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your next witness, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, I call Major Bruurmijn, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much sir. Good morning. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be seated. Mr. Thomas, I see that the witness has given partly his names and some partly his initials can we get the full names on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Major, are you comfortably settled there?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm comfortably settled. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can you begin, Major, please, with your full name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: My full name is Hubertus Johannes Wilhelmus Bruurmijn. My date of birth is 21 December 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And, sir, what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I am a military in the service of the Dutch Defence Services.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: What is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I am a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, we had listed, I think on our list of witnesses as a lieutenant-colonel. I take it that was premature on our part?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, a little of your military background prior to your posting to Sarajevo in 1995.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: In January 1984, I entered -- when I had to do the draft I was the platoon commander of a tank platoon, and during that period I liked it so much that I signed on with the military. In 1987, as platoon commander I was stationed for a reconnaissance platoon in Germany. I was there for four years. In 1991, I returned to the Netherlands and went to a training centre to train others. And in 1993, I went to the School of Military Information Services to train people in combat information services.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And in 1995, Major, were you posted as part of the UNPROFOR force to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I no longer remember the exact date. We initially arrived in Zagreb; I believe that was around 3 April. We spent about two weeks there for some more training, and subsequently some of us went on to Sarajevo, including myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarification. Was the witness a member of UNPROFOR or UNMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And while we are there, what does the acronym SMID stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] School of Military Information Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Following your training or period in Zagreb, how soon thereafter were you posted to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Immediately after the training in Zagreb, which lasted at most two weeks, somewhere between ten days and two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And -- and what role were you posted to in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: As UNMO, so as United Nations Military Observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can you explain, please, for the Trial Chamber what that means.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: As a military observer, you're unarmed and you're part of an international team comprising between 10 and 14 people who were assigned an area to patrol or to observe. I -- you live among the people, so you're not stationed at an UN base, and you have to arrange your accommodations, and from those accommodations either you man an observer post or you patrol the area or you talk to the warring parties. What matters most is to be the eyes and ears of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: So specifically what was your function?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I was a member of an UNMO team, and my main responsibility was to observe and register what happened in the city and to compile a report about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: There was an UNMO organisation sector headquarters in the UN sector headquarters at the PTT building in Sarajevo, and that's where the reports were submitted. Patrol reports were always in writing. Reports of investigations into incidents were also in writing. Only if you were in the observation posts did you submit your reports by radio of shooting incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: All together somewhere between five and six months, except for leave periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you recall the -- the end of the war with the signing of the Dayton Peace Agreement?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The moment the Dayton negotiations started, my mission ended. I believe that the signatures -- it wasn't -- it wasn't signed until I was back in the Netherlands. As far as I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us something about the training you received in Zagreb prior to your arrival in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The training in Zagreb comprised various components, general affairs; for example, to see whether driving skills were adequate. You were taught about connecting Motorola equipment used by the UNMOs. Your English skills were tested and you were trained to analyse craters. So, for example, how you could determine from which angle a grenade had been thrown.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, when you talk about craters, what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Craters, traces that remained behind, either on paved or unpaved surfaces following a grenade that fell and the impact of a grenade or bottom with the consequence of an artillery or mortar grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And, specifically, what was your training in crater analyse designed to enable you to do?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: In crater analysis you learn, first of all, to determine how -- to determine what the trail looks like, what the crater looks like. And the shards have flown away from the point of impact, so you learn to see what the front end of the projection was and then you use two wooden stakes to pull a line down the centre, and then you use a compass to determine the main direction, from which the grenade arrived, from which the impact came. So, essentially, crater analysis teaches you to determine the direction of origin of a grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, the translation I'm getting is that this is in relation to grenades. Was -- was your crater analysis training limited to just an examination of grenade craters or other types of shells?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: It was about explosives that hit the ground from a certain trajectory. They could be mortar or artillery grenades or bombs dropped by air planes as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: During your time in Sarajevo, were you required to conduct crater analyses to determine source or origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. I performed crater analysis both on artillery shootings and mortar shooting and on improvised airplane bombs dropped with MRS rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Could you just explain the term you have just given us, regarding the rockets, Colonel -- Major?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That would be MLRS and that stands for multiple rocket launch system. MLRS and those are ordinarily rockets fired from a vehicle with multiple rockets at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, thank you. I'd like to return to that point a little later on. But, first can you tell us what the -- or describe the situation in Sarajevo when you arrived in late April 1995.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: At that time, a cease-fire was in effect between the warring parties, but shooting incidents regularly erupted between the parties and these shooting incidents on the front lines might last one to ten minutes, and then there was intensive firing. In addition, at that point, many sniper incidents took place, and what was remarkable to me was that the majority or, rather, all victims that we examined were children or elderly people who were clearly present as non-combatants. In other respects the situation was quite surprising in the city because the city had been under siege for three years by then. I expected to arrive in an area where people lived exclusively from shelters, but the population, nonetheless, tried to maintain a normal way of life, although I do have to say that at one moment, things appeared relatively normal in the city; and then, at other moments if there was a threat of shelling or sniping, there would be massive panic, massive fear, and within a minute, the streets could suddenly be empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, just one further point of clarification. You've described events affecting the population of Sarajevo. In what part of Sarajevo are you describing? The part held by which forces?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: My patrol area was limited to the Bosniak area of the city. I was unable to move freely on the Serb side. In addition, the UNMO teams were arranged officially as one team, but one team would have a group on the Serb side and the other part of the team would be on the Bosnian side. I was assigned to the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, you have describe add situation of a cease-fire when you first arrived in Sarajevo. Did that cease-fire last?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No. Some time in late May -- well, you might wonder what is a cease-fire, if firing incidents happened regularly any way. However, by late May, it was clear that the cease-fire was really over. There was one day that both parties fired a lot of mortars and artillery at each other, and from that point onward, it was, once again, an all-out war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: From late May until the end of the war in 1995, was there any change in that situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, following -- or, rather, I believe it was following that day when everybody started firing mortars and artillery again, the UN issued various ultimatums both to the Bosnian and the Serb sides. These concerned stopping the firing and for the Serbs to remove heavy artillery for several kilometres. I don't remember that off the top of my head anymore how many, but also for the Bosnians to place their artillery in storage sites. And at that point, there were NATO air-strikes. At first, only on the Bosnian Serbs and then another ultimatum was issued and UNMOs were taken hostage by the Serbs and then the run-up to Srebrenica started; and during that period, the incidents shifted from sniping to more shooting mortars to the areas, shooting mortars at the areas, excuse me. In July, Srebrenica happened. After Srebrenica, NATO launched massive air-strikes on the Serb installations and then the Croats started up Operation Storm to conquer Krajina and that took us into August and then October; and at that point it became clear that the Serbs were loosing a lot of ground and the Dayton negotiations began. What you see from April and May up to that period, is a build up of hostilities culminating in the massive intervention by NATO an operation storm by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: How did these events that you described affect or not affect what happened in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, there was an effect both on the population, and it also affected the number of incidents that took place in the city. As I said, at first in April and early May there was sniping and incidentally firing interactions on the front line, and then the firing incidents became more intense at the confrontation line. And a Bosnian offensive followed. Initially they gained some ground on the Serbs, but at the end of that day or the day afterwards, the Serbs reversed that. Yes, it certainly affected the population, especially around the fall of Srebrenica. The population felt very much abandoned by the UN, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I object to the -- to the narrative form of the answer as well as I'd like to get some clarification with regard to -- if at all possible the dates that the witness is speaking to. He has mentioned a Bosnian offensive without a date. Apparently that offensive then was rejected, when that occurred we don't know. Then it moved up to the fall of Srebrenica, which is a different issue in a different location. If we could go perhaps -- proceed by question and answer with regard to the general question that Mr. Thomas has asked concerning the -- how the events affected what happened in Sarajevo would be fine. The answer is somewhat vague and elusive in form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Actually what is your objection? You started off by saying you object to the narrative form of the answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I object to the answer being non-responsive to the question asked and specifically, and it's vague with regard to dates, since we're covering a long period of time here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the answer is certainly responsive to the question that I posed. Clearly more specific details are required, but I was allowing the major to complete his answer before we filled in those gaps. But I recognise that we are getting a very long answer from the major, and I can take him step by step, sir, through the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you do recognise that, then cut him short where you think he has given you a sufficient answer to your question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, I'm particularly interested here in the effect upon the civilian population, in terms of how these events translated into any actions, if any, taken against the civilian population of Sarajevo. You described a number of events beginning with the lead-up to Srebrenica and then continuing through to the end of the war. Can you describe for us what happened to the civilian population during that period.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Initially the civilian population was affected especially by the sniping incidents. This instigated fear among the population. There were several sites in the city where there was an elevated risk of being shot if you even appeared there. In the beginning, and I'm talking about April and early May, utilities in the city such as electricity and gas were available, and, of course, that had -- had an impact on the water facilities as well. After the day of intensive shooting, both the gas and the electricity were cut off from the Serb area. So there was virtually no electricity or gas anymore in the city, and, of course, that negatively affected the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, you described shelling that took place between the two forces in May 1995. Was there any other shelling between the two forces in Sarajevo through to the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. From that period in May, shooting was commonplace at the city, so there were two different aspects here. On the one hand, some of the shooting was directed at military targets, or, rather, short-term military targets, so shooting at a confrontation line to achieve a certain objective or at a vehicle that was positioned somewhere to neutralize that vehicle, but then there were also multiple shells that were fired in rapid succession and then there was some other attacks that, in my view, targeted only the civilian population. Those were single-shell attacks or a single bomb directed at places where there were crowds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: How often would these attacks on civilians occur?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I can't give you exact figures anymore. I don't remember that. When I'm referring to generalities, it wasn't daily, but it did happen several times a week; and the majority of those shooting incidents took place in the older section of Sarajevo. That was not the area where I patrolled. I was at the west of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you know what ordnance was used to carry out these attacks against civilians?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The translation is in error.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At this point based upon the witness' previous answer, I'm going to object on the grounds of hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, I can lay a foundation for the question I've asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, as a -- as an UNMO, were you privy to the reports filed by other UNMOs in -- in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. First, you would hear reports over the radio as soon as a shooting incident took place. You could hear that, and all UNMOs were on the same frequency, so you would hear what was happening and where an investigating team had been sent. And in the period of June and July, I spent six weeks at the headquarters or the headquarters sector in Sarajevo as duty officer, and there my responsibility was to set forth in writing reports received over the radio and to draft the daily sitrep and that was also where all written reports were submitted by the teams; and as a consequence that's where I read all filed all written reports as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is a sitrep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A situation report, explaining what transpired that day in terms of general affairs and incidents and predictions as to what lies ahead in the coming period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I request that whenever you use acronyms that were peculiar to your situation you explain them to us, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, then based on your own direct observations and the information you received from other sources, can you describe for us or tell us what type of ordnance was commonly used in the shelling attacks against civilians?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: It -- you mean what kind of munitions? Ordnance is munitions. [In English] Sorry there are some translation problems at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want to switch over to English there.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The English one which I saw on the screen, I can answer that one. Sorry. [Interpretation] The munitions used for shooting if we're talking about the civilian population, consists primary of mortar shells and several times improvised airplane bombs were used that were driven, powered by MLRS. As far as I can remember, I don't remember artillery shells at the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: When did you first encounter air bombs?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: We were aware from the reports that it was happening both around Sarajevo and elsewhere in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's -- it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On or around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1 June or 1 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to object as non-responsive to the question. The question is, When did you first encounter air bombs. Which is to follow up with something else afterwards, that's fine. But the question is quite specific as to when did this witness first encounter air bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I just want to understand what Mr. Guy-Smith --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The answer is non-responsive to the question propounded. The question is when did you first encounter air bombs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that a ground of objection? Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The ground is that the answer is non-responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you objecting to what the witness is saying or are you objecting to what -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The question is fine. I'm saying that the answer is non-responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. Then just wait for your colleague and see what he does with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I did wait for my colleague, and my colleague did nothing with it. And because he did nothing with it, I'm moving to limit the witness' answer when the witness is not responding to the question propounded by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where did you wait, sir? Because the question was asked at page 14, line 8: "When did you first encounter air bombs." "We were aware from the reports that it was happening both around Sarajevo and elsewhere in Bosnia." And at that time -- and at that time you intervened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct because is not responsive to the question. But the question deals with whether he went and encountered. Does it say time specific question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My points is, you didn't wait for your colleague to correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I looked at my colleague, and based upon my perception of my colleague's body language, my colleague was not going to do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith, we don't have the perception of your colleague's body language on the record; so we cannot deal with that at this stage. May you proceed. Objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, if you could continue with your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Before July 1st, all I have is hearsay as to what type of improvised munitions there might be. On 1 July, there was an explosion there Hrasnica, and I went there; and together with a colleague in the Bosnian authorities, I conducted an investigation, and our conclusion based on that investigation, was that that was an air bomb that was fired by MLRS rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Prior to 1st July 1995, through information you received in your capacity as an UNMO, were you aware of air bombs used against the civilian population in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: What are air bombs?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The air bomb we're referring to here are airplane bombs that are ordinarily dropped by an airplane on a target; and in this case, when I am referring to air bombs fired via MLRS rockets, I mean an airplane bomb that MLRS rockets are attached to in some way or another to fire it. So you don't need an airplane to get it to the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: How are they launched, the ones that had been modified in the way you describe?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The way to launch such bombs is that you need some rails that the bombs and rockets are on top of. They're several metres long. They need to be stable because you don't want the rails to drop halfway through the trajectory. The rails will need to be elevated to achieve an ideal angle for launching the bombs -- rockets because in my view, you can't determine accurately the distance that the bombs will travel. There are multiple procedures for doing this. One is to adjust the angle of the launching rails and the other is changing the location from where you are launching, and what we understood about this an once an UNMO explained this to me who had seen one of the trucks is that the rails were mounted on the rear of an open truck; and that sounds logical to me so that you can displace the rails that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Which forces had air bombs?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: We never determined that the Bosnian had them or used them. The only site that we determined they were being launched from were the Serb positions, and my colleague that told me he had seen one of those trucks once, he was on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, the air bombs that were used against the civilians of Sarajevo, which areas did they fall in? Was there a particular area, was it random apparently?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I know that apparently there was an attempt to use air bombs to destroy the TV station. There were various attempts. One landed passed the TV station; two landed in front of the TV station. One hit an apartment building 25 metres from where I had rented a room, and one landed on Hrasnica, and I conducted that investigation, and based on reports from colleagues, at least one and probably others landed in the old area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Compared to, say, a mortar which you have described as having been commonly used when civilians were shelled, what -- what is the destructive power of an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The destructive power is several times greater, if we're talking about a mortar shell that might weigh about ten kilograms. The air bomb used in Hrasnica weighed approximately 230 kilograms so it had a fair greater destructive power. Mortar shell can't destroy a house, but an air bomb, if it lands on a house, will destroy the house entirely and surrounding buildings will also incur heavy damages.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You've touched on this point already, Major, but can they be launched with any real accuracy?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The air bomb that I investigated, there was no -- there was no guiding system to change course after it was launched. Ordinarily a MLRS rocket derives its stability either from rotation or from a different way, and the way that the bomb was attached to the rocket excluded rotation and we didn't find any other traces. In my opinion, it's a highly inaccurate weapon, and if you aim to destroy a specific target, that way you'll need do it by trial and error, simply fire it, see where it lands and launch the next one, fire it, see if you had the same deviation and then correct for that deviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You described the rocket or the air bomb that you investigated as having no guidance system. The other air bomb, the air bombs you have described as having fallen on Sarajevo, are you aware of whether or not any of them had guidance systems?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Do you mean a different one from the one that landed in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You have spoken of number of air bombs that had fallen on Sarajevo while you were there. Did any of those air bombs have guidance systems to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did the witness investigate those? Or go and observe them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think he answered it was from information he received but rather than find that point in the transcript I can cover that with him briefly as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, you described, in addition to the 1 July air bomb which you personally investigated, you described your knowledge of other air bombs which landed on Sarajevo. Were any of those air bomb incidents ones which you personally attended or investigated?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No, I didn't conduct any investigations on those. I did see the report about one of those bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: In relation to that report which you saw, in relation to the other bomb, was there any mention of a guidance system on that air bomb?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No. That report did not mention a guidance system.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: In your dealings with other UNMOs, would you -- would you discuss or share information about air bombs or air bomb incidents?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Were you ever given information that any air bomb had a guidance system on it?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No. The only information about that once I saw photographs of one of those air bombs, that was a different model that the one that landed on Hrasnica. There were no indications that that had a guidance system either. And in discussions, the only thing mentioned that -- was that what was found was only mechanical in the sense that the rockets were attached and apparently it was fired according to the principle of, We'll see where that lands and possibly correct the path. But there was never any question of a guidance system being attached to the rockets or the bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, I'd like to turn now to the 1 July 1995 incident in Hrasnica, of which you've already touched upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is scheduled incident number A8. I wonder if we could have 65 ter Exhibit 2719 on the screen, please. And, Your Honours, this is map 8 in the court binder, the Prosecution court binder that has been provided to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, do you have that match on your screen in front of you? Do you recognise that map?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. That's the map probably at a scale of 1:50.000 of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, at this point, can we please tender the blank map as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Map 8, is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that will be Exhibit P439.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Madam Registrar. And, Madam Registrar, or Mr. Usher, is there a way we can enlarge, please, the bottom two thirds of the map, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: First of all, Major, can you point out for Their Honours where Hrasnica is on that map?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Maybe with the assistance -- we'll do it that way. There is an electronic pen that you use, Major, if Mr. Usher can just provide that to you. And tell us if the need the area enlarged a little more. I think, in fact, that might be useful, Your Honours. Again, the bottom half of the map of Hrasnica, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If we enlarge that area a little more, are you able to pinpoint more accurately the scene of the incident on 1 July 1995? And if you can't, please say so?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I can't do that more accurately. As far as I know that's one of the houses that circles just a tiny bit too high. I think that was one of the houses in the circle. But I cannot tell you 100 percent accurately. I can no longer give the coordinates on the map of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Before we go any further, could you mark the larger circle you have drawn being the area of Hrasnica, with the letter a?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And could you mark the smaller circle, being the area slightly above, as I understand it, the scene of the air bomb impact as -- as B, please.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, six months down the line when we read this map, I'm not -- I can't guarantee I will be able to recognise that structure as an A and a B.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. I agree, Your Honour. I wonder if we could start again. Could we have P439 up on the screen, please, which is the blank map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Ah, perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can you mark with a cross, please, Major, the scene of the impact as best as you can recall it now.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we tender that marked map as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The marked map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P440.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Madam Registrar. Thank you, Mr. Usher, that is it all we need of your services at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: While I'm asking the next series of questions, Your Honours, I wonder if 65 ter 01383 can come up on the screen, page 4 it will take some time to load, so I can use the time with other question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: 01383 and the page that I'm looking for, Your Honours is page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: First of all, when did you arrive at the scene?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: It was in the evening of 1 July 1995. I no longer remember the exact time, but it would have been around 2100 hours, perhaps a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Is the scene in Bosnian-held part of Sarajevo or the Bosnian Serb-held part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: It was in the Bosnian part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the purpose of your attendance at the scene?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Shortly before, there was a radio announcement by Captain Frank Melum of an explosion at his UNMO team site. After that, there were radio reports about injured from his team at that explosion that there was a -- that there was an attack site and that he wanted support at his location and the operations officer, a Danish captain, Hansen, decided that he would head in that direction and he needed somebody to accompany him; and at that precise moment I had finished my duty officer shift, so he asked me to ride with him to Hrasnica, and we -- the two of us got in the car and drove to Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And what did you find when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: There was substantial disorder. You see that on the photographs. The top photograph reveals the site where the bomb exploded. There was a shed garage there where you see the crater, and you can see that the house behind it is seriously damaged. The second photograph, and you see a white car in front of that, that's the UNMO team house. He was staying on the first flight up of that home and the ground floor, the landlord and his family lived; and can you see that that building is seriously damaged. The car in front is an UN car and as can you see it is seriously damaged. Before that, when I arrived, there was still an armoured UN car which was admittedly damaged but still drivable, and there was still quite a few people milling about, and the majority of the UNMO team had been evacuated to the hospital and the UNMO team leader, Captain Frank Melum, was also on site. Also on site was the Bosnian chief of police, together with a police officer. They were present in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I want to take us through that one step at a time please, Captain. Firstly, Major, sorry. Firstly, if we look at the top photograph on the screen and if that could please be enlarged as much as it can be, Mr. Usher. First of all, you described a garage where the bomb had hit. Do we see the garage in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No. The garage is where -- was where you see the crater. That's where the garage was. At least that is what I was told, because you don't really see much left of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And where is the crater? Can we point to the crater, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Before we go -- before we go any further, just dealing with the crater, we see quite a large amount of shadowed area where you have marked with the cross. Are you able on that photograph to -- to basically draw the outline of the crater?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: What I've indicated here are the contours and the general debris that you see, to determine from which direction the shell landed. And I could extend that a bit ... [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Major. We'll come to your crater analysis in a moment. But if we could scroll down, please, to the second photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, just before we do that, by scrolling are we going to loose -- we are, I'm sorry. Could we produce the marked photograph as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The marked photograph is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Madam Registrar. Once that's done, Your Honour, could we please scroll down to the second photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, Major, you describe someone as living in the top floor of that building. You simply described him as he. Can you tell us who occupied the top floor of the building?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Not the top floor. The first flight up, and that's where the UNMO team resided. Under the aegis of Captain Frank Melum.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And on the bottom floor you described the landlord and his family as occupying that building. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And where, in relation to the previous photograph we've looked at, is this house?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Using the previous photograph as a point of reference, this house is to the left of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If we scroll up, please, Mr. Usher, to the first photograph. On the far edge, left hand edge of that photograph, do we see the end of the same building, the UNMO building?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the same house.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we produce this page of two photographs as a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The two photographs are admitted into evidence as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be exhibit P442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: As part of your duties at the scene, were you required to investigate what had caused this damage?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Not at first. Ultimately, however -- no, excuse me. After all, we were there to provide backup for Frank Melum's team but because all his team members were either injured or no longer wanted to remain at that site, I spent the night near Frank, and Frank did indeed have to conduct the investigation of the impact and ordinarily these investigations are conducted with more than one UNMO and I was the only UNMO present, so that is why it was my duty to assist Frank the next morning with the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Were there casualties from this explosion?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. Several UNMOs were injured by glass shards and in the adjacent some people were injured as well. I'm not sure whether there were any casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You mean casualties in the sense of fatalities?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. When did you conduct -- before I move on to the -- before I move on to that. Besides the damage to the building, or buildings, and besides the obvious dealing with those injured, were there -- was there a lot of activity around the scene when you arrived that evening?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: There were still quite a few people out on the street. By then, the police had calmed down and stabilized the area and didn't allow anybody near the crater or into the house because shortly before that, there had been at least two moments at which people tried to attack the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. Which team?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The UNMO team.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Once the area was secured, did you spend the night in the UNMO house with Captain Melum?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I spent the night there. Captain Melum was worried that if he left his team's site he would lose all the materials still present there, given the two previous efforts to attack, so the population was not truly favourably disposed because they assumed that the UNMO team or the UN had been the target of that attack. So the captain was worried that if he abandoned that team location, he would not be able to use that location again, as the location for his team. That's the reason we spent the night there and you wouldn't abandon an UNMO, you wouldn't leave him alone at such a location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: During the course of the evening, we don't need to go into what Captain Melum told you, but during the course of the evening did you discuss with Captain Melum what had occurred with the impact and the aftermath?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. We spent quite a while in the house clearing things up and trying to correct things and damage, and we spoke extensively about what had happened and what the consequences were and what would be possible for the team in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The next morning then, did you and Captain Melum conduct an investigation of the -- of the site?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. We both conducted an analysis of the crater. At first, the local police started analysing the crater, and we attended that and examined what they did and then repeated that for ourselves, so that we would have our own results as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And when you say the local investigators, do you know which organisation or agency they were from?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, the local police. The Hrasnica chief of police was present and his investigators performed the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, in terms of your own investigation, in general terms, what did you do? How did you conduct that investigation?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: First you examined the dispersion pattern from the depth of the crater, and you examine the pattern that the earth displaced the wreckage, and you take a point of reference and from that point of reference you move backward and you can span a line between that and then you use your compass to establish the shooting direction and the path of origin of the projectile; and then you look further into the hole to find shards and other bits to see what type of projectile it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Was -- was this the standard methodology that you had been trained to employ?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, that's how we learned it, and we had received an instructional [as interpreted] map instructing that, if after a while, you didn't know with 100 percent accuracy to do it then you could check your map of instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the time. I'm just about to go into the findings and now would be an appropriate time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at a quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, could we please have 65 ter number 08595 on the screen, please, page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to make a brief remark. I see a small error in the translation on the transcript that appears on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English translation reads an instructional map. The English word shouldn't be instructional map it should be aide-memoire. Map refers to a map, and this is an aide-memoire, so a list of instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, we have a document in English and in B/C/S on the screen in front of you. Is this a document that you were able to review yesterday?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. And this was not a report that you yourself prepared. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: But upon reviewing the contents of this document, and I'm talking about the three pages that constitute the team report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: So I wonder if we could just go through the next -- or just briefly have the next two pages up on the screen as well, Your Honour, please, one after another. And just, finally, the third page of that same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, that is a -- a report that records the observations and comments of the UNMOs who were present at the house at the time of the explosion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Although you yourself did not prepare this report, to the contents, nevertheless, are they consist with what Captain Melum described to you throughout the course of the evening you spent with him and your own observations, both that night and the day after?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'd like to turn, Your Honours, please, to page 7 of the same document, both page 7 in the English and page 7 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's the report following the crater analysis and, as you can see, my signature appears at the bottom right. I signed that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That contains what you found and a record of your findings, in terms of direction of fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct, and that also indicates what type of bomb was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I want you to look at paragraph 2, please. And is there a correction that you would like to maybe to paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. I see there it reads that we believed - how should I put this? - that the bomb and the driving object were deliberately released during the trajectory. I don't believe that's correct. I don't think it was deliberate. I think that the propulsion of the -- was released during the trajectory but that it was not deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Does that correction in any way affect your conclusions as to source or direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No, that would not affect them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I have difficulty with that correction. My difficulty arises from the fact that this -- at the bottom of this report, it is signed by two people and the core author is not here to confirm the correction. What do we do about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Maybe we can -- I can discuss the reason for the correction a little with the Major, sir, and that might allow Your Honours to resolve that conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I doubt it. I think I would need the core author also to confirm the resolution of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I can take it as far as I can with him, sir, and see where that gets us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You've described that the weapon involved was an air bomb and given the details of that particular part of the projectile in your report, and you also described that it had attached to it a rocket assembly made up a pair of three different calibre rockets. Can you explain to us what you found, in relation to the bomb, on the one hand, and the rocket assembly on the other?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: First of all, there were not three different calibres of rockets; there were only two calibres. During the crater analysis, we found only parts of the bomb, no tail piece that would ordinarily be attached to a bomb, exclusively the smooth body of the bomb, nor did we find any item such as electronic devices or other mechanical means to indicate that you want the bottom to do something after a certain period of time, other than the delayed mechanism causing the bomb to explode. The rockets that we found, those were six MLRS rockets, and there was a type of adapter plate that was used to attach the rockets to the body of the bomb, and we did not observe any traces of an explosion there or of anything to ensure a mechanical release. To me, that suggests that there was a -- either a small explosion that separated the two or that there was some timed released mechanism and that's why I don't entirely agree with what I signed at the time in paragraph 2; namely, a deliberate release of -- between the propulsion and the explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If there had been a release mechanism attached to this projectile, would you have expected to have found any traces of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll let it go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As I said previously, you would have needed to see something at the attachment plate that would have attached the rockets to the body of the bomb, or you would have seen traces of a small explosive charge being detonated that separated the two, and nothing along those lines was visible there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If you had found something of that nature, would that have been recorded in a report such as this?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically because that indicates how something is launched or how the distance of such a projectile could be determined. Distance might not be the correct word. It would be the effective conveyance.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, the translation I got was "effective conveyance." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: [In English] Effective conveyance well, I don't know the word conveyance in this setting, but it would be the effective range or range which you want to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please, Your Honours. I'm sorry, we'll need page 9 in the B/C/S. No, my apologies. We have the right page. And if the sketch could please be rotated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that sketch, Major?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Yes, that's a sketch that I drew myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Of?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's the sketch reflecting our assessment of how the complete projectile appeared when it was launched, of which only the air bomb impacted next to the house where the UNMOs were and the base plate that -- and the rockets as they were found, 150 metres in front of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please produce or tender pages 2 through to 8 of 65 ter 8595 as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, all those pages that you are referring to mentioned at various places, various kind of -- kinds of acronyms, which I don't understand. If you look at the team report itself, from the beginning of the report, in the last line of paragraph 2, there's SX acronym. In the next paragraph, there's R2 at SX.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know what R2 is. The next page is R1 and DO at the bottom of the page. These are all acronyms that I'm not going to know what they mean when I do read this report later, and I don't know whether you are able to help us through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I can certainly try to do that, sir. Could we please begin with -- could we please have two up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, Major, you will see in the second-to-last line of paragraph 2, a reference to Captains Melum and Hache. Is that how you pronounce his name?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Helped return them while Captain Silva reported the situation to SX." Do you know what SX stands for?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. Sierra/X-ray was the call sign of the UNMO sector headquarters in Sarajevo, so it was a radio call sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If we go to the second to last line of the next paragraph, there is another reference to Captain Melum calling R2 at SX. Do you know what R2 at SX denotes. We know what SX is; what is R2?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: R2 was the radio call sign of one of the operations officers, Romeo 1 was the call sign of a different operations officer. So those denote officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, please, Madam Registrar, the last line of that page -- sorry the last paragraph of that page, we see the reference to DO.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: DO is the abbreviation denotes duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And in the final line of the same document on the next page, do we see -- I'm sorry, we see the reference to MPs.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: MP is the abbreviation for military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go, please, to page 7, which is your crater analysis. First entry paragraph 1, under paragraph 1 we see grid BP 839, 525. Can you tell us, please, what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Grid Bravo Papa and then the numbers denote the coordinates to 100 metres accuracy on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, the coordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, that is main paragraph 2, not bracket paragraph 2. We have reference to: "The weapon observed in flight by OP 4." What is OP 4?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: OP 4 denotes observation post number 4. That would have been one of the observation posts manned by UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. I hope I have covered them all sufficiently, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you. In which case could we please produce pages 2 to 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Pages 2 to 8 -- sorry. When you say pages 2, do you mean the -- starting from team report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I didn't refer to the cover page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Pages 2 to 8 of that document are admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now we know that your conclusion was that this was an air bomb modified in the way that have you described?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, sorry, Mr. Thomas. Madam Registrar, the transcript says that will be Exhibit 443. Is it 443 or 433?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is 443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 443. Thank you so much. You play proceed, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, can you please explain for us your conclusion as to the line of fire. Where -- what direction had this air bomb come from? And tell us if you need to refer to your analysis.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: First, on the morning of 2 July, we performed the crater analysis and that analysis yielded a direction, and if I'm correct it was between 280 and 320 degrees. The only reason I still remember that is because I re-read the reports again yesterday. My memory is not that great. The place where the rockets were found, so from the propulsion system at approximately 150 metres from where the bomb exploded is along the same lines so between 280 and 320 degrees; and if you carry that through, and look at the observations from the observation post 4, then everything is consistent, and there was nothing contradicting the conclusion that -- that the angle was between 280 and 320.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Are you able to say, having made those findings, where the source of fire was?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That would have been the Ilidza area, which was then in the hands of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I wonder if we could have Exhibit P440 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, you will recognise this as the map you had earlier marked with the impact site. What I'd like to you do is identify for us on the map where you considered the source of fire to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And if we could have the left-hand half of the map blown up, please.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The Ilidza area is approximately that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Would you mark that, please, with the letter I, so we can distinguish it from the other marking that we have there.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And can we produce that, Your Honours, as a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map as marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The map as marked for the second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map as marked for the second time as admitted as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P444.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher, that's ... thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, in the area where the air bomb landed, were there any military targets?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: At the exact site where the air bomb landed were no military targets as far as I know. The only target of military value in the surroundings was the Famos factory where I have heard that the Bosniaks to produce munitions or weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And how far was this area which was hit by the air bomb from the Famos factory?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a precise answer. I would have to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Was it on the same firing line?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I want to look, please, at document number 65 ter 04799, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If we could have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before there's any answer given, I would object to the relevance of this document being shown to this witness at this time and ask for an offer of proof and any arguments to be made be made outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I have no objection. I do want to be heard on the matter, sir. I have no objection to the major leaving the courtroom while we engage in that discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Bruurmijn, can you excuse us for some few minutes. We'll call you back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As I understand the exhibit being shown, this exhibit involves an order dated the 6th of April, 1995 from Dragomir Milosevic. We are dealing with an incident in July of 1995, and based upon a plain reading of the order itself, it has no relevance to the questions that have been asked of this particular gentleman. And specifically, I refer the Court to the order which is to immediately prepare a launcher with an aerial bomb and transport the bomb for launching, and it is in response to specifically the fact that there have been Muslim forces for the past three days attacking various positions. So it is a fact-specific order dealing with an incident-specific issue, is my initial submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to make a full submission, Mr. Guy-Smith, so we don't keep standing up and down again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely. This matter was fully litigated in the Milosevic case, and not only was it fully litigated in the Milosevic case but the specific order which is now been shown to this witness was relied upon by the Prosecution with regard to the shelling of a residential area in Hrasnica on the 7th of April, 1995. In paragraphs 475, the incident itself is discussed in the Milosevic judgement from paragraphs 475 through and including paragraph 495. The specific order which is being presently shown to this witness is noted in footnote 1787 as P226, order by RSK commander to prepare air bomb launcher dated 6 April 1995. So it has been relied upon by the Prosecution for the purpose of dealing with a very specific incident. That incident there has been a finding of in a prior trial before the Tribunal, and it therefore has no relevance whatsoever to these, proceedings, with regard to an incident that occurred months after the order was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Two preliminary points first, Your Honours. The first is that it is not intended to produce this witness -- produce this exhibit or tender this exhibit through this witness. Plainly he is not in a position to authenticate a RSK order. Secondly, Prosecution does not rely on there exhibit or wish to discuss the exhibit with is this witness for the purpose of demonstrating that this order relates to this shelling which occurred on the 1st of July, 1995. The probative value of the exhibit and the relevance of the exhibit lies in establishing that the Ilidza Brigade of the Sarajevo Romanija corps had the capability to launch air bombs from the location described here by Major Bruurmijn, that they had that capability prior to the 1st of July, 1995; and therefore by demonstrating that they had the capability to launch -- that they had air bombs, that they had launchers, that they launched from Ilidza, that they plainly could have launched at Hrasnica because that is actually specifically mentioned in this particular order all provides corroboration for Major Bruurmijn's find that source of fire was Ilidza because the capability can be demonstrated as having existed at Ilidza. My purpose in putting the document to him was to ensure that that is a correct interpretation of that document. To ask him is what is contained in that document consistent with the scenario that you have reported on 1st July. We're not saying it is the same incident, but it is important that if this document is to be relied upon for corroboration that he can say, Yes, what is being described in that document is effectively what did end up happening on the 1st of July. They had that exact capability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So when you say at paragraph 42, line 1: "My purpose in putting the document to him was to ensure that that is a correct interpretation of that document. Which document are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Of the order. In other words, my reading of the order is that the Ilidza Brigade is being asked to launch an air bomb from their position in Ilidza towards Hrasnica. Now I need him to confirm that that happens to be the scenario that he has described as relating to the 1 July 1995 incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he has told us the scenario, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: He has, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand what you say the purpose of tendering this document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just don't understand why you want him to give an interpretation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: This document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. And I agree with that, Your Honour. I do not want to be in a situation, however, where the Prosecution is later relying on this document as corroboration of Mr. Bruurmijn's findings and then being met with the objection well, Major Bruurmijn was never provided or never cross-examined on this particular document, the order, because it was never put to him. He was never asked to confirm, and he was never asked to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Any reply Mr. Guy-Smith? None.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise. I was double-checking what Mr. Thomas just said. I would -- I would never make the objection Mr. Thomas is concerned about because I don't believe the document is relevant for the purposes of this individual's testimony. He told us how he arrived at his conclusions from where the air bomb came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. I guess Mr. Thomas has explained the purpose for wanting to tender this document not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think it is appropriate to come through this witness. I don't think it is relevant as regards to this witness, and I don't think this witness is in a position to speak to the document. If I were to cross-examine the witness about the document - something I would not do - but if I were to do that, I would probably -- I probably be faced with objections with regard to whether or not the information contained in this particular document is information upon which this witness can testify. It's outside the purview of his knowledge, and it is speculative. Any examination with regard to this would be speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done? Thank you very much. You may call the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry about that, Major. Some of the vicissitude in the trial. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, we have a document on the screen which you yourself are not the author of; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now you had the opportunity to read this document yesterday in English; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I want to ask you some -- or a question about this document, but I think given that you're testifying in Dutch, I should read it. It is only a short document so that you get the complete Dutch translation which you did not have yesterday; is that all right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct. I saw only the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. The document is addressed from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command that is headed strictly confidential number 20/04-118, dated 6 April 1995, and addressed to the Ilidza Infantry Brigade. It reads: "For the past three days, Muslim forces have been attacking the positions of the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade and the attacks are particularly pronounced in the sector of the Famos factory. "Several of our soldiers and a large number of civilians have been wounded. "In order to thwart the enemy and give them a warning them so they are forced to accept this truce, I hereby order: "1. The Ilidza Brigade will immediately prepare a launcher with an aerial bomb and transport the bomb for launching. The most profitable target must be selected in Hrasnica or Sokolovic colony where the greatest casualties and material damage would be inflicted. "Inform me personally of the readiness for implementation of this task." And it is signed and stamped by the RSK Major-General Dragomir Milosevic. Major, you gave us your conclusions as to the nature of the weapon, the line of fire, and the source of fire in relation to the air bomb on the 1st of July, 1995. Given those findings, do you have any comment to make in relation to this document that is now on the screen?
