utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, the assignment issued in this order corresponds with what we saw. There's an assignment here to prepare an air bomb for launch and to fire it in the Hrasnica or the Sokolovic area, and the assignment was issued to the Ilidza unit. So all these data correspond with what we found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Major. I have no more questions for you at the moment. My learned friend of the Defence will have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you not tendering this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, it was not my intention to tender it as this witness cannot authenticate the actual order itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Major, I would like to start off where you just left off, with regard to the document that was just up on the screen, and as I understand it, you were given the document while you were involved in a proofing session; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The session yesterday afternoon. Yes, that's correct, or rather, yesterday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And before you were given the document, were any comments made to you about the purpose of you reviewing that document?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was it handed to you in a series of other documents?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yesterday morning, I was presented with multiple documents. This one was among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you read it yesterday morning, after you read it, did you have occasion to comment to anybody concerning what you'd read?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I made a remark about this document to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The man seated at my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For the record -- could you identify for the record, that's Mr. Thomas; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you made a comment concerning this document, what did you tell Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I was surprised that this document existed because from my perception it was extremely stupid as a commander to set this assignment forth in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is that what you told Mr. Thomas yesterday?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you discuss whether or not you would be testifying at all about this document when you came to court?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas told me that he might present this document at the hearing to me the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from telling Mr. Thomas that you thought it was an extremely stupid thing to do, was there any other discussion with regard to your review of this document during your proofing session before you came to court?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas asked me the same question that he did -- that he just asked me here in court, whether this assignment corresponds with -- or correlates with the conclusions I reached following my investigation of the aerial bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I gave him the same answer as I just gave now: Yes, this does correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How long was your proofing session yesterday?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I arrived in this building at about 10.30, and the session lasted until 12.00 or 12.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And after the session was over, was a document compiled for your review and signature concerning the meeting that you'd had with Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct. The signature session took place that afternoon, after 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the document that you read was a document that you read in English; correct? The signature session? You read a document concerning what you had discussed with Mr. Thomas. That document was in English; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You had no difficulty reading that document, now, did you?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you understood the information that was contained in the document as representing a complete recitation of the information that you had discussed with Mr. Thomas during your proofing session; correct? And by complete I don't mean verbatim. I don't mean word for word. I mean topics. It covered topics and articulated the topics that you had discussed with Mr. Thomas; correct? For example, this order. For example, the document that we have been referring to, the one that you believe to be stupid.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I couldn't say with 100 percent accuracy whether that document was listed as well. It wasn't clear to me that the document being compiled was intended as a reflection of everything discussed at the time. We reviewed previous statements of mine and those statements were set forth in writing and I signed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, within the context of the information that you reviewed yesterday and that you discussed with Mr. Thomas, you made some very specific remarks with regard to the 1st of July, 2nd of July, 1995, crater analysis, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you included in that the following, which is the findings of the Bosnian police, your own crater analysis, the radio message of an UNMO who had heard rockets launched from Ilidza the night before enabled you to make a determination about the source and method of fire; right? That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you not include in any manner, shape or form the analysis that you just went through with us today concerning this particular order, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I would direct my -- I'm sorry, Your Honours. If my learned friend has the proofing note, I would direct him to the entries under 65 ter number 4799 on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm looking at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. In that case, I object to the question and the manner that has been put, Your Honour. If my learned friend has a proposition to put to the witness about just how much he spoke or just how much is recorded in the proofing note about this order, then he should put the contents of the proofing note in that respect to Major Bruurmijn first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He has told us that you engaged in a question and answer -- excuse me. I don't wish to argue with Mr. Thomas. The witness has told us that they engaged in a question-and-answer proceeding with regard to this order, and as I am reading this particular document, page 2, I -- if what you are suggesting is the language. The witness confirms this document is consistent with the July 1st scenario as being the sum total of the information. I need some help here from Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You realise that you gentlemen, the three of you, are talking about a document to which the Bench is not privy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it's going to make it very difficult for this Bench to rule on something that we don't know nothing about. We are told that there is a reference to 65 ter 04799 to the extent that we able to determine what that is supposed to mean. This is supposed to be this document that is now in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me give assistance in that regard, Your Honour because I didn't -- I didn't believe I would be in this particular situation today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The proofing note indicates that you confirm that this document is consistent with the July 1st scenario. That's what the proofing note says. When you signed the proofing note, did you understand that to mean that that dealt with the question and answer colloquy that you went through with Mr. Thomas concerning the order of Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, before the witness answers, you had put a proposition to the witness that the document on the screen, which is no longer there, had never been mentioned in the proofing note. Your colleague referred you to the part of the proofing note that refers to 65 ter 04799.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand -- I understand the Court's concern, and I'm modifying the line of examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do have you my question in mind or shall I?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: [In English] No, I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Or -- I thought that might be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 04799 back up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you -- after you read the document and you had made the comment that you had made about the document, which is that you thought it was stupid, you and Mr. Thomas had a conversation concerning potential questions he might ask you and answers you would give concerning this particular document; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a very long question. Mr. Thomas asked me whether it was consistent with the findings established on 1 and 2 July, 1995, and indicated that he might use this document before the Court. I don't remember any more questions that he asked about that document along the lines of, And I'm going to ask you that question tomorrow. He showed me the document and said, I might be using this in court tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you -- when you -- when you saw the document and heard him say that, what was your response to him, with regard to the use of this document? Did you say, Well, this document confirms my findings?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I said that this document corresponded with what I observed on 1 and 2 July, and I expressed surprise at the content of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's what you told us before, with regard to the wisdom of having such a document in existence?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Major Bruurmijn, when you nod, it doesn't get recorded that you are agreeing, so could you also say yes or no to indicate whether you are agreeing or disagreeing.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: From June -- if I understood your testimony correctly. Not from June, in June and July you had the duty to draft daily sitreps for your unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: In that period, I was a duty officer, and one of my tasks was to prepare the daily UNMO headquarters Sarajevo Sector sitrep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was something that you did every day for the month of June and for two weeks in the month of July; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You prepared a specific sitrep concerning the July 1st incident that you investigated; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No. I don't think I was the one who compiled that sitrep, but that was because I was in the field with the UNMO team, and therefore was not at the headquarters as duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have a chance before that sitrep went out to take a look at what was memorialised with regard to the July 1st incident?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No, I did not see Frank Melum compile the draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And have you had an occasion at any time since the July 1st incident to take a gander at that particular sitrep? Sorry gander is a bit informal, take a look at?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. Because from 2 July, I was, once again, active as the duty officer, and all reports submitted in writing were physically present at the Sector HQ in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that -- that the day when everybody started firing mortars and artillery again - this is on page 9 - the UN issued various ultimatums both to the Bosnian and Serb sides.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What ultimatums did the United Nations issue?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise renditions of the ultimatums, but the gist was that the heavy weapons either had to be removed from a certain range around the city. That wasn't possible for the Bosnian side. They didn't control that part of the city. And the Bosnians units had to place their weapons in UN storage sites, and if that didn't happen, then NATO air-strikes might follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware that, on July 2nd, a weekly situation report was issued concerning the question of Bosnian heavy weapons operating from near UNPROFOR facilities having significantly increased.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Not on that specific date, but I know that in that period, the Bosniaks were firing mortars to the Serb side. One of the mortar installations of the Bosniaks was 50 metres next to the PTT building, which were the sector headquarters of the UN in Sarajevo; and I know that they were fired from that position, but I can't give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the PTT building; what does PTT stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Post telegraph and something else. The former postal building in Sarajevo that was -- that during the war was set up as sector headquarters by the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have 1D00-4539, page 3 in e-court. And I'm referring to the bottom of the page. If we could have the very last part of the page where it says location of Bosnian weapons a problem, made a little bit larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is this information, the information that is contained there, which is: "Since the Bosnian offensive began two weeks ago the number of Bosnian heavy weapons operating from near UNPROFOR facilities has significantly increased? "Some people in UNPROFOR see this as an effort by the Bosnians to draw counter-battery fire on to UNPROFOR which would then be drawn into convict with the Serbs. Others note that there has been a general increase in the number of activity weapons and that the density of heavy weapons is not greater around UNPROFOR facilities than it is elsewhere." Is this something that you in your capacity for UNMO as an observer had cause to discuss or have concern about, in terms of trying to make intelligence decisions about what was going on, on a day-to-day basis?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: This was certainly cause for concern among the UNMOs, including me. I just mentioned that a mortar was positioned next to the UN sector headquarters in Sarajevo. The observation post of the team to which I pertained before I became a duty officer and to which I returned afterwards, there was a mortar installation 50 metres away from the observation post. So, yes, we were concerned about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And just for purposes of clarity of the record, I'm sure that my colleague will agree, the date of this report is dated 2nd of July, 1995, and if the Bench would like to see, we can pull up page 1, just so that you can see the date. Looking at the up at the right-hand corner where it says: Date. Could you confirm for us that the date of this report is the 2nd of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in terms of -- in terms of dealing with the issue of ultimatums, were you in a position where you heard that the United Nations was issuing ultimatums with regard to what NATO was going to do, or whether there was some -- the division as between United Nations and NATO, in terms of ultimatums?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The ultimatums issued were issued by the UN to the warring parties because they realised that having an ultimatum and deploying the means mentioned in this ultimatum; namely air-strikes would severely affect the units on the ground. That's why we were informed when an ultimatum was issued and when it would expire. We were given a list with code words that we could refer to when we heard a certain code word. On the radio, for example, we knew that a ultimatum had expired and that within 24 hours, air-strikes might follow; and then there was another code word indicating that an air-strike would ensue within a shorter number of hours. So, yes, we were aware that ultimatums had been issued as well as the time-frame for potential air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us as you sit here today how many ultimatums you recall being issued that passed, before there was ultimately an air-strike? Put in other terms, how many times you heard a code word that says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't hear that; what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Or how many times you heard a code word that said and I went "wheeee," which obviously won't translate on the record, but gave you some relief that there would be no bombing from international forces?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I couldn't tell that anymore. What I remember that is on three occasions ultimatums expired and was followed by air-strikes, but I can't give you an exact number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you given a code word when nothing was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember anymore. We were given code words indicating the number of hours within which something would take place. I don't remember there being a code word that -- to indicate that an operation had been cancelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So if an ultimatum, once again we're speaking a bit hypothetically because you can't remember. But you do recall ultimatums being given; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And are you testifying now that every time you recall an ultimatum being given during your tour in the region, that there was an air-strike?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On those occasions when an ultimatum was given, and there was no air-strike, how did you receive information regarding the fact that the ultimatum had been satisfied, through other negotiations or something else had taken place whereby they were not going to be engaging in air-strikes? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just asked the question and he said no such word was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that he didn't have a code word, so I'm trying to find out if there was some other method of communication they engaged in, apart from just a code word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I can remember is that sometimes ultimatums expired or, rather, you knew the date and the time that the ultimatum was supposed to expire; and sometimes we heard that it had been extended to give parties additional time, but I can't remember any indication that an ultimatum had expired but that no air-strike would follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So if there was a modification of the ultimatum that wouldn't come to you in terms of a code word. That would come to you in some other terms as you said its been extended, or there's been further negotiations, or something else was going on so the ultimatum is not going to take force and effect; right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would this be an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to go to the incident of July 1st, 1995, that you investigated. But before that, just to make sure that I understand your testimony, prior to the July 1st incident, you had never investigated personally an alleged air bomb incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, lest we forget, and now that it is not on the screen any longer. What do you intend doing with ID 004539, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh could I tender that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And before this investigation, the training that you had received with regard to bomb or shelling analysis had been for a period of a couple of weeks; correct? When you first arrived in the region?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you've told us that -- one of the ways that you can determine information concerning where shelling or a bomb has come from is by examining the crater itself; right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There are obviously other manners in which you can determine the direction from which the particular bomb came from. For example, if you saw it flying in the air.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the issue of crater examination, the importance of crater examination, in terms of determining direction of launch, or, I should say this, point of launch, is that the crater itself will have a particular kind of pattern which will assist you in determining how the projectile actually hit the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct. You cannot exactly determine the point of departure. You can only establish from which direction it originated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in terms of -- in terms of establishing from which direction it originated, could you tell us, what are you looking for in terms of crater pattern? What are the indicators that you use to determine direction?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Because the shell or bomb penetrated the ground from a certain angle before exploding, there will be a more acute angle and a sloped angle; and the material blown away by the explosion will be projected in a certain shape and pattern, and those are things you can consider in performing a crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the first thing that you've mentioned, which is the issue of angle, does the angle that the projectile is seen to have entered the crater or the ground, which made the crater. Let me rephrase that. Is the angle by which the projectile has hit the ground an indicator of distance or direction from whence it came?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: If you mean the angle at which the projectile hit the ground, that's an indication for -- for -- steep drop or a slower drop followed and that doesn't provide any indication other than that usually have to deal -- you -- usually you're dealing with a mortar shell if the angle is -- is acute and it's a -- usually an artillery bomb if it's -- if there's a gentler slope of the path.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the angle that we're talking about, that would be -- that would be generally defined as the impact angle; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the angle of impact assists in determining the distance that the projectile travelled before impact?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The angle of impact but then again depending on what type of projectile it is, whether it was a ballistic trajectory or a propelled explosive, in this case, it was propelled, the projectile was propelled; and then it's more complicated to determine based on the impact angle what distance was travelled because you can recalculate it in ballistic terms but not if the object was propelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So if the object is propelled, what factors do you use in order to determine the distance that the object travelled before impact?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: There is no way to determine the distance in the case of a propelled projectile. All you can do is establish the direction of origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Whereas in the other form of projectile you can determine distance, I take it?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: You can use ballistics to determine the distance travelled by an artillery shell and the distance from which it was launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So we're clear, it was an artillery shell you can determine the distance; but when it is propelled, based on crater analysis, you cannot determine distance; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: With an artillery shell you could determine the distance. I can't do that because I don't have ballistics training. You need quite a bit of mathematical knowledge. What we checked when we examined the impacts was merely the direction from which the shell or bomb had been launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now with regard to that, what you looked at, was among other things, the impact angle in which the bomb hit the ground and the impact angle is what you have described in that crater; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Now the problem is which angle do you mean. The impact angle is the angle of impact on the ground, so that enables you to determine what was the front and what was the rear of the shell, when you determine the angle it arrived at. But the elevation angle matters less. It is it purely about determining the front and the rear so that you can set your compass accordingly to determine the direction. So whether it impacts at 45 or at 60 degrees that angle doesn't matter. What matters is what was the front and what was the rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please pull up 443. I believe it's page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, by 443, do you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Exhibit 443, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the investigation that you engaged in, the impact angle is not known; right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Right. We didn't determine the impact angle, and that wasn't what we were looking for either. We were looking to establish the direction of origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that. You say with regard to the impact angle, you say: "The impact angle is unknown, as the bomb struck a small concrete garage." So are we to take it that this means that what happened is when the bomb hit, the first thing it hit was a small concrete garage?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The garage had a concrete floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- I'm reading what -- what the document say, sir. That's all I'm doing. And it says: "The bomb struck a small concrete garage." It doesn't say anything about a floor, does it?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct. As far as I remember, the floor was made of concrete, not the rest of the garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- is the photograph that we saw previously -- and I'm sorry, I forgot the ... I believe it is P441.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have that up on the screen for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is the photograph that you took of the crater a photograph that reflects damage to the concrete floor of the garage that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: As far as I know, this is not the photograph that I took myself but the one taken by the Bosnian police. My photographs and negatives are in the possession of the Yugoslavia Tribunal, but I don't see them in the evidence here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Does this photograph, then, to the extent that it is of some help to us, does this photograph reflect the concrete floor area that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And is --

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: You don't see much left of that. It was just that I had been told there had been a garage there. Frank Melum told me that. Because as you can see on the photograph here, there is little traces left that there was any building at all of this site.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know -- I appreciate that. But do you know what the course of impact was of this particular bomb before it hit the concrete floor area? Do you know what it went through beforehand? Did it go through a concrete roof, did it go through a tile roof, did it go through a wooden roof? Can you tell us what the height was of the roof when it first -- the bomb first hit it? Could give us any of that information?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Negative. I do not have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the photograph we are looking at here, this photograph, you can't see any patterns of any explosion, can you? So this photograph is not of assistance to us in determining the front or back of the bomb, looking at the concrete area.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I disagree. If you look at the shadow section you'll see that that's steeper than the area facing the photographer, so that indicates to me that the photograph was -- excuse me, the bomb arrived roughly along the path over the shoulder of the photographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it that what you're telling us is that this photograph is taken from a position where the photographer is looking directly on to -- looking directly towards the house. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct. The photographer is facing the house next door here, and if you look at the background, you'll see Mount Igman or the foothills of Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you present when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are your photographs any more detailed, in terms of the impact zone themselves than this photograph is, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I couldn't say anymore. I surrendered those photographs in 1996, and I saw them one time after that in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Inaudible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I don't have those photographs anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You didn't have a chance to see those photographs yesterday, did you?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I saw these photographs that are included here. I didn't see my own photographs again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you have no knowledge as to where your photographs are?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I know that the Yugoslavia Tribunal still has them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. When you arrived at the bombing location, did you determine whether or not it had an address? And by that, I mean did you ever come across anybody identifying the address as being on Bunici Potok Street?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever determine for yourself what the address was of this bomb site?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No. In the military, you work less with addresses than with map coordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you -- so the answer would be, no, you didn't determine that.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No, I did not determine the address.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The first time that you were there was on the 1st of July, in the evening hours, correct, sometime after 9.00?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you got there after a brief survey of the situation, you made a determination with one of your fellow officers to go to the hospital to check on the rest of your group; right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you left and went to the hospital to check on your group, who was stationed at the house? Who was stationed at the bomb site, securing the area?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was Captain Hansen, and -- then I accompanied Captain Melum to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So Captain Hansen remained behind. You went to the hospital, and after you returned from the hospital, you returned to the bomb site area, right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How long a period of time were you gone?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I think it would have been a maximum of 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The next day on the 2nd of July, would it be fair to say that there was a joint and independent investigation going on concerning this particular bombing? And by joint and separate I mean that you in your capacity as UNMO were engaged in an investigation; at the same time there were BiH police investigators present?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: We were present while the Bosnian police conducted their investigation. They didn't allow us to investigate first. And after the Bosnian police had completed the investigation, we conducted our own investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when the Bosnian police conducted their investigation, did they share with you the fact that they had found damage in an area approximately some 150 metres away from where you were investigating. As a matter of fact, that's where they found the rockets; right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it was the Bosnian police that found the rockets, not UNMOs who found the rockets correct?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the first time that you saw the rockets was at the police station; true?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see a photograph of the position of the rockets in situ at the time that they were first discovered by the Bosnian police?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Did you discuss with the Bosnian police their analysis that the air bomb had hit an area approximately 150 metres away and then ricochetted over to the area where you ultimately found the bomb?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. There was some discussion about that. The Bosnian police assumed at first that there had been two rocket impacts. Where they found the rocket bodies, they thought that was the second impact site. We indicated, in part, because of the observations by OP 4 that only one rocket had been launched, and at that the site where the rockets had been found, no shell fragments appeared and, on the other hand, where the bomb impact was, we didn't find any rocket components; so our conclusion was that the two had -- belonged -- they belonged together. The Bosnian police was not convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What about the issue concerning the ricochet, that the bomb, in fact, hit an area 150 metres away from where it ultimately landed?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That would be possible that it impacted the ground first and then ricochetted onward because I wasn't able to investigate that place. I can't tell you whether that option is more or less probable. My expectation was that it fell apart in the air so that the rockets landed away from the bomb, but even with the ricochet theory, you would need to examine the site where the rockets impacted; and the Bosnian police didn't allow us to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. With regard to the ricochet theory to the extent that the ricochet theory was something that was being discussed, did you take into account in the trajectory paths that you were hypothesising the angle of ricochet from the area that the rockets were found, approximately 150 metres away to where the bomb was found? Did you take that into account in any fashion whatsoever? And I understand that you weren't able to go to the actual area, but did you include that in your calculation?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: At first we recalculated the path based on the crater analysis we had performed, combined with the observations of OP 4 of a rocket that they heard and/or saw, and if you draw a straight line along that path, the rockets would still be -- the place where we found the rockets was still along that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You just added an additional factor, which is that OP 4 heard or saw. So I'd like it talk to you for a minute about the issue of sound. Now, could you tell us at what speed does this projectile travel, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Based -- based upon your information, can you tell us anything with regard to the sound or sounds and period of time that they lasted or were heard by OP 4?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No. I believe that one of the reports mentions a report by OP 4 but I can no longer recollect whether they saw or heard it. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would the period of time in which one was able to identify sound be a factor that could be utilised for determining distance from point of launch? Put in other terms: The speed of sound has a particular formula; correct? So if you hear something you can make some determination of the distance that is travelled?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Well, can you use sound but then you also need visual observation to establish how far away from you something took place. If you have sound alone, then, as far as I know, distance is impossible to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the issue of the demolition capability and destructive capability of this particular device, do you recall previously stating -- in a previous statement that the damage radius was 200 metres which you then corrected to 60 metres. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: I recall that we discussed the radius of the damage. We examined the damage in the immediate proximity. You can see that in the photographs of the damage. At a larger distance, so exceeding 60 metres, windows were shattered, but we didn't investigate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would the fact that -- as a theoretical matter, would the fact that the bomb hit point number 1 and then ricochetted for 150 metres and then hit point number 2, effect the damage potential of the bomb on impact?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. And that depends primary on how the explosive's timer is set. If the detonator is set too quick, then it might explode at the first point of impact, but this one had a delaying device so that the bomb wasn't detonated until several seconds after the impact. So in that case, yes, it does make a difference how it impacts and where it impacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps you could help me out here, because I'm a little confused. Is the type of bomb that we're talking about here, is that a concussion warhead projectile or is that a projectile that operates on a delayed fuse?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: This had a delayed fuse but that doesn't exclude it from being a concussion projectile. It was specially designed to penetrate further into a target before detonating. To give you an example if you have a bomb with a quick detonator then it would explode the moment it touched the edge of a branch. This one didn't. It was designed for maximum penetration before exploding. And that's what the UNMOs state in their report. First they heard a loud bang and thought that something had fallen over somewhere, and after about ten seconds, they heard the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it's that particular information upon which you rely for this to have been a delayed fuse bomb, right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's part of the information. The other part of the information consisted of the shards dug up from the crater because for a penetration bomb, the front end of the bomb has to be quite firm so that it doesn't fall apart as soon as it hits something; and that was the case with this bomb. At the time I had Dutch manuals with me, describing all munitions in use in the former Yugoslavia, and based on the shards and the descriptions in the book, I examined what corresponded with what, and that's how I come up with the delayed fuse and what the -- what other possibilities there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber as you sit here today in any fashion whatsoever what you believe the distance that this particular bomb travelled was?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No, I couldn't -- I couldn't assess that. We depended on the observations of OP 4 to do the best we could. Based on the crater analysis we could determine only the originating direction, and with improvised explosives such as this one, I can't estimate how far it would travel from the moment it was launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you can't -- apart from the issue concerning the potential ricochet theory, you can't give us, as you sit here today, based often your investigation, the angle of descent of this particular bomb, right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Lastly, I wanted to briefly touch on the issue of guidance systems. And you said during your direct examination was that there were no guidance systems on any of the air bombs that you ever heard about, and there was not a guidance system on this air bomb; right?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as I understood -- as I understood your answer, you were talking about a guidance system which was attached to the rocket or the bomb; correct? That's what you told us. You said there was never any question of a guidance system being attached to the rockets or the bomb. It's on page 19 and 20.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: We didn't find any traces of something having been attached to that bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, during that time in the history of artillery, there weren't any guidance systems that were attached to any shells, mortars, rockets, or bombs that corrected the path of such a projectile during flight, were there?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Well, there are and there were at the time too. If we're talking about artillery munitions, for example, there were copper head munitions which are fired and then they second charge to seat their target. They did exist, and we're not talking about an artillery shell here. This is an air bomb. Air bombs have been equipped for some time with guidance systems. For example, the AGM 88 or similar series. During World War II, the Germans were also experimenting with guidance systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: An AGM 88 is not an air bomb that you would launch off the back of a truck, is it?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No. But that -- the 230-kilogram air bomb that we're talking about was not initially that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was the air bomb that was the subject of the incident on July 1st, 1995, launched from a plane?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: No. My assessment is that it was launched from a rail and was propelled by six rockets attached at the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that during the time you were in Sarajevo, none of the incidents, be they bombs or shelling, involved missiles that had in- flight guidance. Excuse me, change missiles to projectiles that had in-flight guidance systems used by the Bosnian Serbs or by the Bosnian Muslims during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: The only air bombs used and dropped by airplanes during the time that I was there were dropped by NATO planes and undoubtedly included munitions that were guided. As for munitions used by the Bosnians and the Bosnian Serb sides, munitions were used, but these were anti-tank rocketed; and they were used in the city as well, and there was a guidance system there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that the anti-tank rocket system that was used had an in-flight guidance system that was used by the Bosnians and the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Any re-examination, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Major, would an air bomb of the type you investigated on the 1st of July propelled by the rockets you found make a lot of noise in flight?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Given that we're all civilians, apart from yourself, is there anything you can compare it to so that we can understand how much noise we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to describe the noise. The best description would be a jet engine operating at full speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just before we conclude, Exhibit 65 ter number 4799 about which there has been a lot of discussion already this morning, in case it is to be used later, it should probably be MFI'd. I don't know that we did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We did not because I specifically asked you and you said you were not tendering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Not at this stage, Your Honour, and I misunderstood Your Honour's question and I wasn't thinking about the need to MFI the document. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. Then -- yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That makes good sense to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. 65 ter 04799 is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P445, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Does that conclude your re-examination Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It does, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one question that I would like to ask, Major, and you may have answered this, but I just want to be sure that I hear the answer again. On this theory of a ricochet, what would the bomb have hit that caused it to ricochet?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: To cause a ricochet, it would have had to impact something hard, as opposed for example to soft ground. If it had impacted soft ground, it would have penetrated immediately. Ricochetting requires relatively hard substratum and that could be either a road or a house, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From this distance of 150 metres where you were not allowed to go, sitting where you are you, are you able to think of any object that is so hard that would have caused it to ricochet?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: There were houses and roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But we see here it destroyed the houses here at the tail-end. It didn't ricochet when it hit this house, this garage here; and you're saying that this garage had a concrete floor, which I would expect to be even harder than the wall of a house.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Yes. If it had encountered the wall a house, the object that it impacts that's hard needs to be horizontal or not at a very steep angle because otherwise it would -- it wouldn't ricochet. When it hits an upright wall it would penetrate. So to ricochet, you need a hard horizontal surface.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A hard horizontal surface.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what kind of hard horizontal surface can you think of that was existing at that time, some 150 metres away?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: It could be a house under construction without a roof but with a very thick concrete floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A concrete floor would not be horizontal, sir, it would be longitudinal.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's what I mean when I say horizontal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, horizontal can't mean longitudinal. The two are opposite.

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Horizontal is, as you see the table in front of me. It would ricochet from that vertical, depending on the angle it was projecting along, it would ricochet from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you aware of any buildings that had no roofs around the area but which had concrete floors?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Not specifically in that area. I know that one of the ways at the time in former Yugoslavia to avoid property taxes was to never finish building your house. So many houses were inhabited but were not complete yet, and sometimes they didn't have a roof, merely the concrete top -- of the top floor, so to speak. So there were houses with a flat concrete top but whether they were any in that area, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, would it be your testimony that, on the basis of the ricochet theory it would hit the concrete floor of an incomplete building somewhere, ricochet to this garage that it destroyed, and penetrate the concrete floor of this garage and not ricochet again? Would that be your testimony?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: That's correct. The ricochet theory is not necessarily my theory. I still consider it possible that it would ricochet from a hard concrete substratum depending on the thickness of the concrete. The moment it would ricochet, according to that theory, it would still be flying at a considerable speed because the rockets were still attached but after the ricochet, it no longer had any propulsion and the speed would diminish and that all influenced whether something penetrates or ricochets. I'm not a scientist. It seems plausible to me. However, my theory remains that because of the construction and because it was an improvised device, it simply fell apart in mid-air and the bomb continued somewhat further than the rockets. But I can't exclude a ricochet theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That very last sentence that you make, that you can't exclude a ricochet theory, causes me concern simply because the former part of your answer seems to say -- to say that the ricochet theory is not -- is not plausible. Or didn't I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: HUBERTUS JOHANNES WILHELMUS BRUURMIJN
utterances.text: Then I'm afraid that you misunderstood me. In my opinion, it is possible but it seems less likely to me. What seems most likely to me is that it fell apart in mid-air, but I can't exclude that it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions arising, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you answer, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much, Major, for coming to testify. You are now excused and may go now well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Alstublieft. Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: So that concludes the evidence that the Prosecution can put before Your Honours today. I believe it also concludes the evidence that we can put before you this week given the personal medical difficulties that arose in relation to a witness schedule for tomorrow and which I believe the Chamber has been notified of. So we are able to proceed again on Monday, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that event, the matter stands adjourned to Monday, the 19th of January, at 9.00, not at quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom II. Okay? 9.00, Courtroom II, 19th of January. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th of January, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
